title: Finding bugs in Raft implementations | Antithesis
excerpt: Why formal verification is not enough to maintain consensus in real systems
content_html:
Introduction

TW Lim Technical Writer

The Raft consensus protocol is one of the foundations of the internet. Raft offers a formal specification in TLA+ and a concrete, detailed implementation guide, and hundreds of groups have created open-source implementations of the algorithm by following the instructions in the guide. It is, by far, the most widely used consensus algorithm in production systems.

Despite the paper’s famously accessible style, we’ve found bugs in every Raft implementation we’ve tested, including HashiCorp Raft, Aeron Cluster, OpenRaft, and MicroRaft — despite the investment in formal methods, careful code review, unit testing, and years of testing in production. The bugs we found manifest as violations of Raft’s main invariant (called state machine safety in the paper, commonly referred to elsewhere as total order delivery). If you’re using a Raft implementation, you might want to check it for bugs.

We’ve sent bug reports upstream. This isn’t intended as a critique of Raft, its authors, its implementers, or any particular implementation. Raft implementations, even with a formal specification and a detailed implementation guide, are not easy to write.

Rather, this is a story about correctness in distributed systems — the inevitability of bugs, the inadequacy of any single approach, and the high cost of learned helplessness.

This is a long post. The first section is a position paper, but the rest is a detailed analysis of the issues we found, using one implementation as an example, a discussion of how we found them, and why we think they’re there.

Why this matters

If you’ve worked on distributed systems, you’ve been part of a war room at some point (if you haven’t, don’t worry, you will be), dealing with an outage like this one, or this one — both of which were caused by consensus failures. When a consensus issue results in an incident, it’s inevitably far reaching and extremely painful to root cause, replicate, and fix. Many consensus issues remain “unsolved”, because they evade reproduction.

It’s hard to know exactly what the real world consequences of these problems are, because consensus protocols sit so low in the stack. Are they corrupting the archive of someone’s personal D&D game? Security risks at a nuclear plant? Delaying trains in Germany? It all depends on where the protocol’s deployed.

What’s certain is that these bugs are a colossal waste of developer time, and affect millions, if not hundreds of millions, of users.

Yet we accept consensus issues and other deep distributed systems bugs as a fact of life — but once upon a time we accepted cholera, and waiting for your turn on the mainframe, as facts of life as well. Developers deserve something better. Everyone who depends on the software we write deserves something better.

Bugs are not a fact of life

We have long accepted consensus bugs as inevitable because consensus protocols are just really, really hard to test properly. To really, thoroughly test a Raft implementation — or any distributed system — you effectively need to imagine every possible thing that could go wrong in your entire stack, and write a test to see if it will break your consensus protocol. It’s virtually impossible to write enough tests to provide this kind of assurance in critical systems.

We get around this in two ways. First, we inflict the testing on our users, in the form of outages, downstream bugs, war rooms, and so on. It’s impossible for a team of developers to write enough tests, but with enough deployments and enough users across enough system configurations, you’re eventually going to find all the problems.

Second, we rely on formal verification, and this is how consensus algorithms are built today. We define a model that we can mathematically prove to be correct, and then we… translate this perfect, platonic thing into code. Most Raft implementations are built this way.

There are degrees here. The Raft protocol is one of very few consensus protocols that meets the strictest standard of “formal verification,” with a manual proof, a model check, and a mechanized proof-of-correctness. Every public consensus protocol we’re aware of has a manual proof/written correctness argument, but only Raft, Paxos, and MultiPaxos have mechanized proofs.

Specifications are not code

Formal verification is a great starting point, in that it helps confirm that a core design is sound. Implementing a distributed consensus protocol without starting from a formal spec would result in many orders of magnitude more bugs than any Raft implementation has.

Conversely, one might wonder what the FoundationDB team might have done if they’d started with a formal spec.

But the issues here demonstrate the difficulties inherent in going from a formal specification to actual production code. As long as the implementations are being done by unreliable, imperfect programmers (whether humans or LLMs), the actual code, and the systems using it, will only be as solid as the implementors’ assumptions — not the formally verified model.

Furthermore, formal specifications are rarely truly complete — in the case of Raft, the TLA spec covers the core protocol, but doesn’t speak to details like installSnapshot, or replica replacement, or handling network packet corruption.

Testing can actually be simple

Surfacing these bugs didn’t require particularly deep knowledge of consensus or distributed systems. We found these using a simple approach, which a junior engineer could implement in less than a day, literally the simplest state-machine replication workload we could come up with. The key is that this is happening while the system is running in Antithesis, subject to the kind of faults that happen in a real world environment.

We want to emphasize this point because all too often, we encounter a learned helplessness around testing complex systems. Our profession thinks (with some justification) that writing tests for distributed systems requires more expertise, time, or tokens than we have. This results in a state of perpetual under-testing, which in turn results in extraordinary amounts of developer time being wasted on firefighting (to say nothing of the mental and emotional exhaustion).

Developers deserve something better. Everyone who depends on the software we write deserves something better.

Testing Raft

Marco Primi Distributed Systems Engineer

About Antithesis

Antithesis is an autonomous testing platform that runs distributed systems in a deterministic simulation environment, with randomly generated inputs, under aggressive fault injection. To use Antithesis, you deploy a full distributed system to the simulation environment along with a workload — a client that drives the system under test.

Antithesis exposes the system under test to the kind of unpredictable turbulence it will experience in production, within the safety of a simulation environment. By randomizing the inputs and faults, and intelligently searching the state space of the system to see if system invariants are ever violated.

We maintain an internal curriculum of systems and bugs we use to benchmark Antithesis’ bug-finding performance. We’ve been adding consensus benchmarks to the curriculum, so we’ve been testing a lot of Raft implementations.

Part of the difficulty of building something unique is that you also need to build a way to measure its performance.

About Raft

A common architectural pattern in distributed systems is state machine replication (SMR): all replicas in the system run copies of the same deterministic state machine, and the same sequence of commands is delivered to all of them to transform the data/state. This causes the replicas to progress in soft-lockstep — the state after applying N commands is consistent across all replicas, and all replicas eventually apply all commands.

Distributed databases (FoundationDB, Aerospike, etc.), message queues (Kafka, NATS, etc.), key-value stores (etcd, Zookeeper), blockchains (Bitcoin, Ethereum), and many other systems are based on SMR.

A fundamental requirement for implementing SMR is that all replicas must receive the same set of commands in the same order — total order delivery. Total order delivery is simple to describe, but hard to architect in the face of network turbulence, process crashes, and disk failures.

Because total order delivery needs to be guaranteed for SMR to work, most systems rely on one of a handful of messaging abstractions, with atomic broadcast, also known as total order broadcast, being the most common. Raft is viewed as the friendliest atomic broadcast protocol, Paxos and viewstamped replication are also in wide use.

Our testing approach

To test a Raft implementation, we run a 3-node Raft cluster in Antithesis with a simple workload we call Chain of Blocks.

Chain of Blocks tests Raft’s most important invariant: after N commands are applied, the state of all replicas matches. It consists of two trivially simple components:

  • A single-state state machine that just hashes the bytes of incoming commands. After each applied command, the state consists of <number of commands applied, current hash>. This is sufficient to allow us to observe state divergence between replicas.
  • A stateless client whose only responsibility is submitting new commands that consist of random arrays of bytes.

You can read more about this workload, and see a sample implementation, here.

Components like Raft are developed and reviewed by experts and battle-hardened by years of exposure. So it’s striking to us that this single, simple testing strategy — that a junior engineer could write in an afternoon (or Claude could write for a handful of tokens) — still finds bugs when it’s run in Antithesis.

Results

In all cases, network partitions and turbulence were sufficient to surface examples of divergence (i.e. no node kill/restart required, or disk corruption, or other faults)

Here’s an example snippet from logs that shows a state machine divergence:

After applying 243 blocks, the hashes of all replicas matched (0x01fd753a). Node1 then applies a different 244th command from Node2 and Node3 (0x2ad8d… vs 0xc92fb…). This results in a different state hash after 244 commands applied (0xfaf6ba1e vs 0xdab0977c), violating the primary safety property of Raft (and the underlying atomic broadcast): that all replicas apply the same sequence of command in the same order.

As an example, here’s a detailed look at the bugs we’ve found in one notable open-source Raft implementation during this process. We emphasize that we’ve found similar bugs in other implementations as well, but are going deep rather than broad here and only presenting one set of bugs to keep the length of this post somewhat manageable.

We plan to update this post with details of bugs in the other Raft implementations we’ve worked with.

HashiCorp Raft

Rohan Padhye Research Fellow

HashiCorp Raft is a mature, popular open-source Raft implementation, and the foundational consensus engine underpinning widely-used production infrastructure tools like Consul, Nomad, and Vault.

We do not believe HashiCorp Raft is any less reliable than the other implementations we tested, or that the bugs in HashiCorp Raft are more serious than the bugs in other implementations — they all violate the same core property of state machine safety.

We found three distinct bugs in total: one causes numerous safety violations (i.e., data divergence as described above) and two cause liveness violations (where some nodes or the whole cluster cannot make progress unless an operator intervenes). The Chain of Blocks implementation we used is here.

Technical primer on Raft

To better understand the nature of these bugs, we should define some terms used frequently in the Raft paper:

  • “Term”, “Leader”, “Follower”, “Election” + “RequestVote” RPC: Raft ensures consensus among a cluster of distributed nodes by dividing the protocol into strictly increasing terms starting with term=1. In each term, the nodes attempt to elect exactly one node as the leader by taking a majority vote; all other nodes are called followers. Leader election is conducted using a remote-procedure call (RPC) called RequestVote.
  • “Log”, “Commit”, “Replication” + “AppendEntries” RPC: Each node maintains a replicated log of data entries (e.g., the commands issued by clients), some prefix of which is said to be committed; that is, the node’s state machine is updated when an entry commits. When a client sends some command to the cluster, only the current leader can service this request, and the leader replicates the associated data entry to all its followers via an RPC called AppendEntries. When a majority of nodes in the cluster have replicated the same data entry in their logs, the leader commits it to its own state machine and broadcasts this fact to its followers. If some follower nodes fall behind because of network faults, or if their entry logs have uncommitted data from previous terms, then the current leader can always catch them up via more AppendEntries RPCs. The AppendEntries RPC is also used as a regular heartbeat mechanism to broadcast that a leader is active.
  • “Compaction”, “Snapshot” + “InstallSnapshot” RPC: When the entry log grows too large, a Raft node can choose to compact all the committed entries in the log and only store on disk a snapshot of the state machine until that point. If a leader node needs to replicate data entries to followers via AppendEntries but its log has already been compacted, it can instead issue an InstallSnapshot RPC to transit the entire state machine to the follower.

Bug 1 - Broken Consensus due to Async Heartbeats

This is the most serious bug we have found. It can affect four of the five safety properties from the Raft paper (Figure 3):

  • Log Matching (violated through mechanism A - seen in the report above)
  • Leader Completeness (violated through mechanism A - seen in the report above)
  • State Machine Safety (violated through mechanism A - seen in the report above)
  • Election Safety (violated through mechanism B - not in the report shown above)
  • Leader Append-Only (not violated)
Root Cause and Trigger
  • The Raft paper assumes that all the operations (handling RPCs, client requests, elections, etc.) are atomic and don’t interleave with each other. Essentially, every node in the protocol is a finite-state machine.
  • In HashiCorp raft, most state-changing operations are handled by a big switch-loop in the main thread, with several other floating goroutines doing async work that should not affect protocol state (e.g., peer-peer “replication” routines for dispatching append-entries, and per-connection “transport” goroutines that listen for incoming RPCs and hand them off to the main thread for processing).
  • EXCEPT there is an optimization that diverges from the protocol: incoming heart-beat messages (i.e., AppendEntries without an entry) are handled on the I/O “transport” thread itself, instead of queuing it up for the main thread’s loop like with other RPCs. Presumably, this is to quickly reset the keep-alive timers and reduce spurious re-elections.
  • CAVEAT is that an incoming heart-beat message (like any other AppendEntries RPC) can change the state if it carries a new term when someone else was elected leader, and this bumps up the global currentTerm which everything else in the main thread relies on, and also sets the current state to be FOLLOWER. It is definitely not sound to perform these state changes concurrently with the main thread, and it can lead to different types of race condition bugs.
Mechanism A - Incoming heartbeat races with dispatchLogs() on main thread

Here’s how the bug causes divergence in a 3-node setup A/B/C:

  • Assume the network link between node A and node B is down.
  • Node A becomes candidate for term T, requests votes (eventually gets it from Node C)
  • Node B also runs for term T but no votes
  • Node B becomes candidate for term T+1, requests votes (gets it from Node C)
  • Node B wins election for term T+1
  • Node A wins election for term T (just received the old vote from Node C)
  • Node B sends out heart-beat AppendEntries with term=T+1, which Node A doesn’t immediately receive
  • Node A gets a client request to apply a new data entry X, and it still thinks it is a leader for term T, so on the main thread it prepares to create a log entry (data=X, term=T) and send out AppendEntries to peers.
    • HOWEVER: Just before it can create the log entry, the heart-beat from Node B sent in step 7 above reaches, setting currentTerm=T+1. Because this is done on the fast-path on the network-transport thread, it races with the main thread.
    • The main thread ends up preparing a log entry (data=X, term=T+1) and also dispatching AppendEntries with these values before the next main-loop iteration where it realizes it is actually now a follower for term T+1.
  • Things get really bad from here. Some nodes apply this bogus data=X, term=T+1 to their logs, while others follow whatever Node B (the true leader for term T+1) says, e.g., they might apply data=Y at the same index with term=T+1. Logs diverge in data but get committed since all say term T+1 for the same index. State machines diverge.
Mechanism B - Incoming heartbeat races with requestVote() on main thread

The same bug can cause another kind of safety violation when the async heartbeat handler races with a concurrent handler for the RequestVote RPC on the main thread. If both the incoming heartbeat and the RequestVote carry higher-numbered but different terms T1 and T2 respectively — this is possible when the receiver just recovers from a fault and is catching up to queued messages from peers — and if T1 is less than T2, then it is possible for the receiver to (i) realize the heartbeat’s term T1 is higher than its current term, then (2) on the main thread processing RequestVote realize that T2 is higher than its current term and so set its current term to T2 and then grant a vote; and then (3) back on the heartbeat handler’s thread set its current term to the lower value T1. Needless to say, it should never be possible for a node that has granted a vote for term T2 to regress its current term back down to a lower value T1! When this node at some later point increments its term to T2 again, it has no memory of the fact that it has already voted in this term.

In summary, the race can eventually cause a node to grant two votes in the same term (T2 above), which in the worst case can lead to two different nodes being elected as leader in the same term! Bug 2 - Deadlock after Leadership Transfer

This bug causes a liveness issue — a leader node is unable to service client requests or commit new entries while the cluster is healthy. The root cause is a deadlock during a leadership transfer operation (a Raft protocol extension used by Consul where you can ask a current leader to transfer leadership to someone else, say for upgrades) that does not immediately signal any warnings but bites you way into the future by getting the whole cluster stuck.

  • When you initiate a leadership transfer from A to B the current leader A first tries to get B’s logs up to date via an async replication thread.
  • The leadership transfer logic is a separate goroutine that waits for this replication before telling B to take over.
  • While all this is happening, A might have to step-down as leader for unrelated reasons (e.g., the lease timer runs out, or it cannot reach a quorum due to network) and say another node C becomes leader.
  • When A steps-down as leader, it aborts all replication threads (including the A—>B catchup) but the leadership transfer goroutine is still blocked waiting for it to complete (an implementation bug).

There is no problem so far, because C is the new leader and it does its job for a while.

  • Unfortunately, the leadership transfer goroutine in A has set a global flag “leadership transfer in progress” and this flag cannot be unset until it is unblocked… but it never will be!!!
  • Crucially, this flag does not prevent it from participating in elections and the flag does not get reset if it wins a future election.
  • So in the future, A can legitimately get re-elected as leader but it will refuse to accept any client requests and stall on future commits with the reason “leadership transfer in progress”.
  • When the network is healthy and A is a leader, there is no way to get out of this other than rebooting the node A to clear the flag.

We caught this using an Antithesis eventually test command that checks for commit progress after fault injection is turned off.

Bug 3 - Livelock in Snapshot Installation

This bug causes a liveness issue: a follower node becomes unable to replicate log entries and is effectively not able to participate in the consensus protocol. The bug can also cause resource exhaustion, where the node starts creating a potentially unbounded number of temporary snapshot files on disk.

The root cause for this bug is painfully simple: in the version of HashiCorp Raft we tested, the implementation of the InstallSnapshot RPC simply does not follow Rule 7 from Figure 13 in the Raft paper which handles the case when an incoming snapshot represents a state that diverges from the receiver’s uncommitted log entries. In the paper, Rule 7 says:

“discard the entire log”

HashiCorp Raft does not discard the existing log, and so after installing the snapshot its state machine can, in some cases, disagree with the data in its own (stale) log entries.

At first, this might sound benign because the state machine should be the final source of truth. However, when the node receives a subsequent AppendEntries RPC from the leader, it faithfully implements a part of the protocol (Rule 2) that says: “[reject AppendEntries] if log doesn’t contain an entry at prevLogIndex whose term matches prevLogTerm”. So, because of the stale logs, the follower rejects subsequent AppendEntries, causing the leader to respond with a new InstallSnapshot, and this cycle goes on forever.

We caught this using an Antithesis eventually test command that checks for state-machine convergence after fault injection is turned off. Sample logs from a test run look like this:

Reflections

TW Lim Technical Writer

If there is a single lesson to be learned here, it’s that formal methods alone cannot ensure that software works, because the formal specification still needs to be implemented, and even if you have mechanized verification, you’re verifying the model and not the implementation itself.

We believe formal methods are useful and necessary — they can confirm the basic soundness of a design, and provide a map that saves engineers from many of the errors that can arise in the implementation of a complex system.

But as these bugs show, errors continue to arise when translating the formal specification to production code. In the course of our work with various Raft implementations, we identified a number of assumptions in the Raft paper that remain implicit. An implementer who misses any of these details is likely to run into trouble.

Assumption 1: Each node is a synchronous process

Marco Primi Distributed Systems Engineer

The paper implicitly assumes that each node is a synchronous process, performing atomic state transitions when handling RPCs and updating its own internal state. The TLA+ spec is designed as such.

At the same time, none of the implementations we’ve looked at have actually been a synchronous process, and there’s no explicit guidance in the implementation guide as to whether and how one can deviate from the synchronous design.

Consider the following situation: Can a leader with an outstanding RPC request respond to a vote, or does it need to wait for a response||timeout? Or should it respond, shut down the request and disregard a future response in order to stay correct?

HashiCorp Raft is mostly synchronous in handling RPCs, with a single thread in a select loop, except when it isn’t — it does asynchronous heartbeat handling, bypassing its main loop, and this is what allows Bug #1 to creep in.

Assumption 2: Each response can be mapped to a request

In the Raft paper, every call is made using RPC, which means that every response can be mapped to a request.

If one implements Raft on top of simple TCP or UDP, and doesn’t realize that request/response correlation is a crucial part of correctness, bad stuff can easily happen.

If you’re not working in a language with a nice RPC library, it’s not obvious how to establish this correspondence. For example, the Raft authors have a simulation on their website, which for obvious reasons is often considered a demo/canonical implementation even though they’ve never described it as such. But even their own implementation deviates from the protocol and includes an extra matchIndex field in the AppendEntries response in order to avoid matching requests to responses.

Assumption 3: currentTerm and votedFor are consistent

Rohan Padhye Research Fellow

Figure 2 of the Raft paper states:

One key assumption is that currentTerm and votedFor are consistent, because the latter records the vote in the current term. If these go out of sync bad things can happen, especially if votedFor is null.

For safety, the writing of these values to persistent storage should be done atomically. But in the protocol, these values actually change at different places, so ensuring that both values are updated together is subtle.

The online simulator in JavaScript does not actually distinguish persistent state from in-memory state, so there is no “reference implementation” of how to do this.

HashiCorp Raft, for instance, deviates from the protocol and non-atomically stores three separate values for currentTerm, lastVoteTerm and lastVoteCand, with a worst-case risk to performance but not safety (i.e., it might persist an updated lastVoteTerm and then crash before updating lastVoteCand, but when it restarts it will just have a pre-determined vote for that term instead of choosing a candidate as normal).

Assumption 4: The entire protocol is formally verified

Figures 2 and 13 in the Raft paper state, respectively:

Rule 2 for AppendEntries and Rule 6 for InstallSnapshot creates a potential pitfall. If you implement this naively when you have discarded your log because of a previous InstallSnapshot, you end up doing the wrong thing (most likely creating infinite loops of RPCs between leader and follower, as I have painfully discovered).

The Raft TLA+ spec and the authors’ simulation don’t actually include InstallSnapshot (though Diego Ongaro’s PhD thesis does discuss the nuances in more depth), so different implementations use different workarounds. HashiCorp Raft, for instance, just avoids discarding logs altogether — which led to Bug #3 above.

Bug #2 above, the deadlock, is in a feature called “leadership transfer” which is an extension to the core protocol. Like InstallSnapshot, this feature was never formally verified in the TLA+ spec.

Conclusion

TW Lim Technical Writer

We have long accepted bugs as inevitable. Distributed systems are almost impossible to test thoroughly because their state spaces are so large, and as our stacks get more complex, the problem only gets worse.

But technological progress also moves the frontier of what’s possible. We ended cholera in the developed world by building water treatment plants and sewage systems. We no longer wait for mainframes because we’ve made computing power cheap and abundant.

The abundance of compute is a recent phenomenon. It’s held true for maybe the last 15 years, less than a tenth of the history of computing. It’s spurred, among other things, the recent surge of interest in formal verification — the hope that mechanized proof and model checking can finally become easy enough, and cheap enough, that we’ll be able to apply these approaches wherever we need. But what our experience with Raft has shown is that implementations of even mechanically proven models can have flaws, because there’s no mechanical way to check the implementors’ assumptions.

Fortunately, cheap and abundant compute has also made it possible to test software in ways we couldn’t before. And the other thing our testing of Raft has shown is that when you run systems under fault, even basic testing methods reveal issues that would once have taken months of manual testing to find.

Developers deserve something better, and so does everyone who depends on our software.

Distributed databases (FoundationDB, Aerospike, etc.), message queues (Kafka, NATS, etc.), key-value stores (etcd, Zookeeper), blockchains (Bitcoin, Ethereum), and many other systems are based on SMR. A fundamental requirement for implementing SMR is that all replicas must receive the same set of commands in the same order — total order delivery. Total order delivery is simple to describe, but hard to architect in the face of network turbulence, process crashes, and disk failures. Because total order delivery needs to be guaranteed for SMR to work, most systems rely on one of a handful of messaging abstractions, with atomic broadcast, also known as total order broadcast, being the most common. Raft is viewed as the friendliest atomic broadcast protocol, Paxos and viewstamped replication are also in wide use. Our testing approach To test a Raft implementation, we run a 3-node Raft cluster in Antithesis with a simple workload we call Chain of Blocks. Chain of Blocks tests Raft’s most important invariant: after N commands are applied, the state of all replicas matches. It consists of two trivially simple components: A single-state state machine that just hashes the bytes of incoming commands. After each applied command, the state consists of <number of commands applied, current hash>. This is sufficient to allow us to observe state divergence between replicas. A stateless client whose only responsibility is submitting new commands that consist of random arrays of bytes. You can read more about this workload, and see a sample implementation, here. Components like Raft are developed and reviewed by experts and battle-hardened by years of exposure. So it’s striking to us that this single, simple testing strategy — that a junior engineer could write in an afternoon (or Claude could write for a handful of tokens) — still finds bugs when it’s run in Antithesis. Results In all cases, network partitions and turbulence were sufficient to surface examples of divergence (i.e. no node kill/restart required, or disk corruption, or other faults) Here’s an example snippet from logs that shows a state machine divergence: [node1]: Applied block 244 (2ad8d...) state: 01fd753a => faf6ba1e[node2]: Applied block 244 (c92fb...) state: 01fd753a => dab0977c[node3]: Applied block 244 (c92fb...) state: 01fd753a => dab0977c After applying 243 blocks, the hashes of all replicas matched (0x01fd753a). Node1 then applies a different 244th command from Node2 and Node3 (0x2ad8d… vs 0xc92fb…). This results in a different state hash after 244 commands applied (0xfaf6ba1e vs 0xdab0977c), violating the primary safety property of Raft (and the underlying atomic broadcast): that all replicas apply the same sequence of command in the same order. As an example, here’s a detailed look at the bugs we’ve found in one notable open-source Raft implementation during this process. We emphasize that we’ve found similar bugs in other implementations as well, but are going deep rather than broad here and only presenting one set of bugs to keep the length of this post somewhat manageable. We plan to update this post with details of bugs in the other Raft implementations we’ve worked with. HashiCorp Raft Rohan Padhye Research Fellow HashiCorp Raft is a mature, popular open-source Raft implementation, and the foundational consensus engine underpinning widely-used production infrastructure tools like Consul, Nomad, and Vault. We do not believe HashiCorp Raft is any less reliable than the other implementations we tested, or that the bugs in HashiCorp Raft are more serious than the bugs in other implementations — they all violate the same core property of state machine safety. We found three distinct bugs in total: one causes numerous safety violations (i.e., data divergence as described above) and two cause liveness violations (where some nodes or the whole cluster cannot make progress unless an operator intervenes). The Chain of Blocks implementation we used is here. When run with Antithesis for just one hour of testing, we see a report that looks like this: Technical primer on Raft To better understand the nature of these bugs, we should define some terms used frequently in the Raft paper: “Term”, “Leader”, “Follower”, “Election” + “RequestVote” RPC: Raft ensures consensus among a cluster of distributed nodes by dividing the protocol into strictly increasing terms starting with term=1. In each term, the nodes attempt to elect exactly one node as the leader by taking a majority vote; all other nodes are called followers. Leader election is conducted using a remote-procedure call (RPC) called RequestVote. “Log”, “Commit”, “Replication” + “AppendEntries” RPC: Each node maintains a replicated log of data entries (e.g., the commands issued by clients), some prefix of which is said to be committed; that is, the node’s state machine is updated when an entry commits. When a client sends some command to the cluster, only the current leader can service this request, and the leader replicates the associated data entry to all its followers via an RPC called AppendEntries. When a majority of nodes in the cluster have replicated the same data entry in their logs, the leader commits it to its own state machine and broadcasts this fact to its followers. If some follower nodes fall behind because of network faults, or if their entry logs have uncommitted data from previous terms, then the current leader can always catch them up via more AppendEntries RPCs. The AppendEntries RPC is also used as a regular heartbeat mechanism to broadcast that a leader is active. “Compaction”, “Snapshot” + “InstallSnapshot” RPC: When the entry log grows too large, a Raft node can choose to compact all the committed entries in the log and only store on disk a snapshot of the state machine until that point. If a leader node needs to replicate data entries to followers via AppendEntries but its log has already been compacted, it can instead issue an InstallSnapshot RPC to transit the entire state machine to the follower. Bug 1 - Broken Consensus due to Async Heartbeats This is the most serious bug we have found. It can affect four of the five safety properties from the Raft paper (Figure 3): Log Matching (violated through mechanism A - seen in the report above) Leader Completeness (violated through mechanism A - seen in the report above) State Machine Safety (violated through mechanism A - seen in the report above) Election Safety (violated through mechanism B - not in the report shown above) Leader Append-Only (not violated) Root Cause and Trigger The Raft paper assumes that all the operations (handling RPCs, client requests, elections, etc.) are atomic and don’t interleave with each other. Essentially, every node in the protocol is a finite-state machine. In HashiCorp raft, most state-changing operations are handled by a big switch-loop in the main thread, with several other floating goroutines doing async work that should not affect protocol state (e.g., peer-peer “replication” routines for dispatching append-entries, and per-connection “transport” goroutines that listen for incoming RPCs and hand them off to the main thread for processing). EXCEPT there is an optimization that diverges from the protocol: incoming heart-beat messages (i.e., AppendEntries without an entry) are handled on the I/O “transport” thread itself, instead of queuing it up for the main thread’s loop like with other RPCs. Presumably, this is to quickly reset the keep-alive timers and reduce spurious re-elections. CAVEAT is that an incoming heart-beat message (like any other AppendEntries RPC) can change the state if it carries a new term when someone else was elected leader, and this bumps up the global currentTerm which everything else in the main thread relies on, and also sets the current state to be FOLLOWER. It is definitely not sound to perform these state changes concurrently with the main thread, and it can lead to different types of race condition bugs. Mechanism A - Incoming heartbeat races with dispatchLogs() on main thread Here’s how the bug causes divergence in a 3-node setup A/B/C: Assume the network link between node A and node B is down. Node A becomes candidate for term T, requests votes (eventually gets it from Node C) Node B also runs for term T but no votes Node B becomes candidate for term T+1, requests votes (gets it from Node C) Node B wins election for term T+1 Node A wins election for term T (just received the old vote from Node C) Node B sends out heart-beat AppendEntries with term=T+1, which Node A doesn’t immediately receive Node A gets a client request to apply a new data entry X, and it still thinks it is a leader for term T, so on the main thread it prepares to create a log entry (data=X, term=T) and send out AppendEntries to peers. HOWEVER: Just before it can create the log entry, the heart-beat from Node B sent in step 7 above reaches, setting currentTerm=T+1. Because this is done on the fast-path on the network-transport thread, it races with the main thread. The main thread ends up preparing a log entry (data=X, term=T+1) and also dispatching AppendEntries with these values before the next main-loop iteration where it realizes it is actually now a follower for term T+1. Things get really bad from here. Some nodes apply this bogus data=X, term=T+1 to their logs, while others follow whatever Node B (the true leader for term T+1) says, e.g., they might apply data=Y at the same index with term=T+1. Logs diverge in data but get committed since all say term T+1 for the same index. State machines diverge. Mechanism B - Incoming heartbeat races with requestVote() on main thread The same bug can cause another kind of safety violation when the async heartbeat handler races with a concurrent handler for the RequestVote RPC on the main thread. If both the incoming heartbeat and the RequestVote carry higher-numbered but different terms T1 and T2 respectively — this is possible when the receiver just recovers from a fault and is catching up to queued messages from peers — and if T1 is less than T2, then it is possible for the receiver to (i) realize the heartbeat’s term T1 is higher than its current term, then (2) on the main thread processing RequestVote realize that T2 is higher than its current term and so set its current term to T2 and then grant a vote; and then (3) back on the heartbeat handler’s thread set its current term to the lower value T1. Needless to say, it should never be possible for a node that has granted a vote for term T2 to regress its current term back down to a lower value T1! When this node at some later point increments its term to T2 again, it has no memory of the fact that it has already voted in this term. In summary, the race can eventually cause a node to grant two votes in the same term (T2 above), which in the worst case can lead to two different nodes being elected as leader in the same term! Here are some sample log messages from HashiCorp Raft when we have observed this race condition and its violation of election safety: 20:11:59.941133 [DEBUG] node-1: vote granted: from="node-2" tally=2 term=286 [...] 20:11:59.941133 [INFO] node-1: election won: tally=2 term=286 [...] 20:11:59.944273 [DEBUG] node-0: vote granted: from="node-2" tally=2 term=286 [...] 20:11:59.944274 [INFO] node-0: election won: tally=2 term=286 Bug 2 - Deadlock after Leadership Transfer This bug causes a liveness issue — a leader node is unable to service client requests or commit new entries while the cluster is healthy. The root cause is a deadlock during a leadership transfer operation (a Raft protocol extension used by Consul where you can ask a current leader to transfer leadership to someone else, say for upgrades) that does not immediately signal any warnings but bites you way into the future by getting the whole cluster stuck. When you initiate a leadership transfer from A to B the current leader A first tries to get B’s logs up to date via an async replication thread. The leadership transfer logic is a separate goroutine that waits for this replication before telling B to take over. While all this is happening, A might have to step-down as leader for unrelated reasons (e.g., the lease timer runs out, or it cannot reach a quorum due to network) and say another node C becomes leader. When A steps-down as leader, it aborts all replication threads (including the A—>B catchup) but the leadership transfer goroutine is still blocked waiting for it to complete (an implementation bug). There is no problem so far, because C is the new leader and it does its job for a while. Unfortunately, the leadership transfer goroutine in A has set a global flag “leadership transfer in progress” and this flag cannot be unset until it is unblocked… but it never will be!!! Crucially, this flag does not prevent it from participating in elections and the flag does not get reset if it wins a future election. So in the future, A can legitimately get re-elected as leader but it will refuse to accept any client requests and stall on future commits with the reason “leadership transfer in progress”. When the network is healthy and A is a leader, there is no way to get out of this other than rebooting the node A to clear the flag. We caught this using an Antithesis eventually test command that checks for commit progress after fault injection is turned off. Bug 3 - Livelock in Snapshot Installation This bug causes a liveness issue: a follower node becomes unable to replicate log entries and is effectively not able to participate in the consensus protocol. The bug can also cause resource exhaustion, where the node starts creating a potentially unbounded number of temporary snapshot files on disk. The root cause for this bug is painfully simple: in the version of HashiCorp Raft we tested, the implementation of the InstallSnapshot RPC simply does not follow Rule 7 from Figure 13 in the Raft paper which handles the case when an incoming snapshot represents a state that diverges from the receiver’s uncommitted log entries. In the paper, Rule 7 says: “discard the entire log” HashiCorp Raft does not discard the existing log, and so after installing the snapshot its state machine can, in some cases, disagree with the data in its own (stale) log entries. At first, this might sound benign because the state machine should be the final source of truth. However, when the node receives a subsequent AppendEntries RPC from the leader, it faithfully implements a part of the protocol (Rule 2) that says: “[reject AppendEntries] if log doesn’t contain an entry at prevLogIndex whose term matches prevLogTerm”. So, because of the stale logs, the follower rejects subsequent AppendEntries, causing the leader to respond with a new InstallSnapshot, and this cycle goes on forever. We caught this using an Antithesis eventually test command that checks for state-machine convergence after fault injection is turned off. is a single lesson to be learned here, it’s that formal methods alone cannot ensure that software works, because the formal specification still needs to be implemented, and even if you have mechanized verification, you’re verifying the model and not the implementation itself. We believe formal methods are useful and necessary — they can confirm the basic soundness of a design, and provide a map that saves engineers from many of the errors that can arise in the implementation of a complex system. But as these bugs show, errors continue to arise when translating the formal specification to production code. In the course of our work with various Raft implementations, we identified a number of assumptions in the Raft paper that remain implicit. An implementer who misses any of these details is likely to run into trouble. Assumption 1: Each node is a synchronous process Marco Primi Distributed Systems Engineer The paper implicitly assumes that each node is a synchronous process, performing atomic state transitions when handling RPCs and updating its own internal state. The TLA+ spec is designed as such. At the same time, none of the implementations we’ve looked at have actually been a synchronous process, and there’s no explicit guidance in the implementation guide as to whether and how one can deviate from the synchronous design. Consider the following situation: Can a leader with an outstanding RPC request respond to a vote, or does it need to wait for a response||timeout? Or should it respond, shut down the request and disregard a future response in order to stay correct? HashiCorp Raft is mostly synchronous in handling RPCs, with a single thread in a select loop, except when it isn’t — it does asynchronous heartbeat handling, bypassing its main loop, and this is what allows Bug #1 to creep in. Assumption 2: Each response can be mapped to a request In the Raft paper, every call is made using RPC, which means that every response can be mapped to a request. If one implements Raft on top of simple TCP or UDP, and doesn’t realize that request/response correlation is a crucial part of correctness, bad stuff can easily happen. If you’re not working in a language with a nice RPC library, it’s not obvious how to establish this correspondence. For example, the Raft authors have a simulation on their website, which for obvious reasons is often considered a demo/canonical implementation even though they’ve never described it as such. But even their own implementation deviates from the protocol and includes an extra matchIndex field in the AppendEntries response in order to avoid matching requests to responses. Assumption 3: currentTerm and votedFor are consistent Rohan Padhye Research Fellow Figure 2 of the Raft paper states: One key assumption is that currentTerm and votedFor are consistent, because the latter records the vote in the current term. If these go out of sync bad things can happen, especially if votedFor is null. For safety, the writing of these values to persistent storage should be done atomically. But in the protocol, these values actually change at different places, so ensuring that both values are updated together is subtle. The online simulator in JavaScript does not actually distinguish persistent state from in-memory state, so there is no “reference implementation” of how to do this. HashiCorp Raft, for instance, deviates from the protocol and non-atomically stores three separate values for currentTerm, lastVoteTerm and lastVoteCand, with a worst-case risk to performance but not safety (i.e., it might persist an updated lastVoteTerm and then crash before updating lastVoteCand, but when it restarts it will just have a pre-determined vote for that term instead of choosing a candidate as normal). Assumption 4: The entire protocol is formally verified Figures 2 and 13 in the Raft paper state, respectively: Rule 2 for AppendEntries and Rule 6 for InstallSnapshot creates a potential pitfall. If you implement this naively when you have discarded your log because of a previous InstallSnapshot, you end up doing the wrong thing (most likely creating infinite loops of RPCs between leader and follower, as I have painfully discovered). The Raft TLA+ spec and the authors’ simulation don’t actually include InstallSnapshot (though Diego Ongaro’s PhD thesis does discuss the nuances in more depth), so different implementations use different workarounds. HashiCorp Raft, for instance, just avoids discarding logs altogether — which led to Bug #3 above. Bug #2 above, the deadlock, is in a feature called “leadership transfer” which is an extension to the core protocol. Like InstallSnapshot, this feature was never formally verified in the TLA+ spec. Conclusion TW Lim Technical Writer We have long accepted bugs as inevitable. Distributed systems are almost impossible to test thoroughly because their state spaces are so large, and as our stacks get more complex, the problem only gets worse. But technological progress also moves the frontier of what’s possible. We ended cholera in the developed world by building water treatment plants and sewage systems. We no longer wait for mainframes because we’ve made computing power cheap and abundant. The abundance of compute is a recent phenomenon. It’s held true for maybe the last 15 years, less than a tenth of the history of computing. It’s spurred, among other things, the recent surge of interest in formal verification — the hope that mechanized proof and model checking can finally become easy enough, and cheap enough, that we’ll be able to apply these approaches wherever we need. But what our experience with Raft has shown is that implementations of even mechanically proven models can have flaws, because there’s no mechanical way to check the implementors’ assumptions. Fortunately, cheap and abundant compute has also made it possible to test software in ways we couldn’t before. And the other thing our testing of Raft has shown is that when you run systems under fault, even basic testing methods reveal issues that would once have taken months of manual testing to find. Developers deserve something better, and so does everyone who depends on our software.

blocks.html_en: Antithesis is an autonomous testing platform that runs distributed systems in a deterministic simulation environment, with randomly generated inputs, under aggressive fault injection. blocks.html_en: A common architectural pattern in distributed systems is state machine replication (SMR): all replicas in the system run copies of the same deterministic state machine, and the same sequence of commands is delivered to all of them to transform the data/state. This causes the replicas to progress in soft-lockstep — the state after applying N commands is consistent across all replicas, and all replicas eventually apply all commands.

sentences.en: A common architectural pattern in distributed systems is state machine replication (SMR): all replicas in the system run copies of the same deterministic state machine, and the same sequence of commands is delivered to all of them to transform the data/state.
sentences.zh: 分布式系统中的常见架构模式是状态机复制（SMR）：系统中的所有副本都运行同一确定性状态机的副本，并且将相同的命令序列传递给所有副本以转换数据/状态。

sentences.en: This causes the replicas to progress in soft-lockstep — the state after applying N commands is consistent across all replicas, and all replicas eventually apply all commands.
sentences.zh: 这会导致副本以软锁步方式进行 - 应用 N 个命令后的状态在所有副本中保持一致，并且所有副本最终应用所有命令。

blocks.html_en: Distributed databases (FoundationDB, Aerospike, etc.), message queues (Kafka, NATS, etc.), key-value stores (etcd, Zookeeper), blockchains (Bitcoin, Ethereum), and many other systems are based on SMR.

sentences.en: Distributed databases (FoundationDB, Aerospike, etc.), message queues (Kafka, NATS, etc.), key-value stores (etcd, Zookeeper), blockchains (Bitcoin, Ethereum), and many other systems are based on SMR.
sentences.zh: 分布式数据库（FoundationDB、Aerospike等）、消息队列（Kafka、NATS等）、键值存储（etcd、Zookeeper）、区块链（比特币、以太坊）和许多其他系统都是基于SMR的。

blocks.html_en: A fundamental requirement for implementing SMR is that all replicas must receive the same set of commands in the same order — total order delivery. Total order delivery is simple to describe, but hard to architect in the face of network turbulence, process crashes, and disk failures.

sentences.zh: 实现 SMR 的一个基本要求是所有副本必须以相同的顺序接收相同的命令集——全序交付。

Raft is viewed as the friendliest atomic broadcast protocol, Paxos and viewstamped replication are also in wide use.

blocks.html_en: • The Raft paper assumes that all the operations (handling RPCs, client requests, elections, etc.) are atomic and don’t interleave with each other. Essentially, every node in the protocol is a finite-state machine.

blocks.html_en: • EXCEPT there is an optimization that diverges from the protocol: incoming heart-beat messages (i.e., AppendEntries without an entry) are handled on the I/O “transport” thread itself, instead of queuing it up for the main thread’s loop like with other RPCs. Presumably, this is to quickly reset the keep-alive timers and reduce spurious re-elections.

blocks.html_en: The same bug can cause another kind of safety violation when the async heartbeat handler races with a concurrent handler for the RequestVote RPC on the main thread. If both the incoming heartbeat and the RequestVote carry higher-numbered but different terms T1 and T2 respectively — this is possible when the receiver just recovers from a fault and is catching up to queued messages from peers — and if T1 is less than T2, then it is possible for the receiver to (i) realize the heartbeat’s term T1 is higher than its current term, then (2) on the main thread processing RequestVote realize that T2 is higher than its current term and so set its current term to T2 and then grant a vote; and then (3) back on the heartbeat handler’s thread set its current term to the lower value T1. Needless to say, it should never be possible for a node that has granted a vote for term T2 to regress its current term back down to a lower value T1! When this node at some later point increments its term to T2 again, it has no memory of the fact that it has already voted in this term.

sentences.en: If both the incoming heartbeat and the RequestVote carry higher-numbered but different terms T1 and T2 respectively — this is possible when the receiver just recovers from a fault and is catching up to queued messages from peers — and if T1 is less than T2, then it is possible for the receiver to (i) realize the heartbeat’s term T1 is higher than its current term, then (2) on the main thread processing RequestVote realize that T2 is higher than its current term and so set its current term to T2 and then grant a vote; and then (3) back on the heartbeat handler’s thread set its current term to the lower value T1.
sentences.zh: 如果传入的心跳和 RequestVote 分别携带编号较大但不同的术语 T1 和 T2（当接收方刚刚从故障中恢复并正在追赶来自对等方的排队消息时，这是可能的）并且如果 T1 小于 T2，则接收方可能 (i) 意识到心跳的术语 T1 高于其当前术语，然后 (2) 在处理 RequestVote 的主线程上意识到 T2 高于其当前术语，因此将其当前术语设置为T2然后授予投票权；然后 (3) 返回心跳处理程序的线程，将其当前项设置为较低的值 T1。

sentences.en: Needless to say, it should never be possible for a node that has granted a vote for term T2 to regress its current term back down to a lower value T1!
sentences.zh: 不用说，对术语 T2 进行投票的节点永远不可能将其当前术语回归到较低的值 T1！

sentences.en: When this node at some later point increments its term to T2 again, it has no memory of the fact that it has already voted in this term.
sentences.zh: 当该节点在稍后某个时刻再次将其任期增加到 T2 时，它不记得自己已经在该任期中投票了。

blocks.html_en: Bug 2 - Deadlock after Leadership Transfer

sentences.en: Bug 2 - Deadlock after Leadership Transfer
sentences.zh: Bug 2 - 领导权转移后陷入僵局

blocks.html_en: This bug causes a liveness issue — a leader node is unable to service client requests or commit new entries while the cluster is healthy. The root cause is a deadlock during a leadership transfer operation (a Raft protocol extension used by Consul where you can ask a current leader to transfer leadership to someone else, say for upgrades) that does not immediately signal any warnings but bites you way into the future by getting the whole cluster stuck.

sentences.en: This bug causes a liveness issue — a leader node is unable to service client requests or commit new entries while the cluster is healthy.
sentences.zh: 此错误会导致活性问题——在集群正常运行时，领导节点无法服务客户端请求或提交新条目。

sentences.en: The root cause is a deadlock during a leadership transfer operation (a Raft protocol extension used by Consul where you can ask a current leader to transfer leadership to someone else, say for upgrades) that does not immediately signal any warnings but bites you way into the future by getting the whole cluster stuck.
sentences.zh: 根本原因是领导权转移操作（Consul 使用的 Raft 协议扩展，您可以要求当前领导者将领导权转移给其他人，例如升级）期间的死锁，它不会立即发出任何警告信号，而是让整个集群陷入困境，从而让您陷入未来。

blocks.html_en: • When you initiate a leadership transfer from A to B the current leader A first tries to get B’s logs up to date via an async replication thread.

sentences.en: When you initiate a leadership transfer from A to B the current leader A first tries to get B’s logs up to date via an async replication thread.
sentences.zh: 当您启动从 A 到 B 的领导权转移时，当前领导者 A 首先尝试通过异步复制线程使 B 的日志保持最新。

blocks.html_en: • The leadership transfer logic is a separate goroutine that waits for this replication before telling B to take over.

sentences.en: The leadership transfer logic is a separate goroutine that waits for this replication before telling B to take over.
sentences.zh: 领导权转移逻辑是一个单独的 goroutine，它在告诉 B 接管之前等待此复制。

blocks.html_en: • While all this is happening, A might have to step-down as leader for unrelated reasons (e.g., the lease timer runs out, or it cannot reach a quorum due to network) and say another node C becomes leader.

sentences.en: While all this is happening, A might have to step-down as leader for unrelated reasons (e.g., the lease timer runs out, or it cannot reach a quorum due to network) and say another node C becomes leader.
sentences.zh: 当这一切发生时，A 可能不得不因为不相关的原因（例如，租约计时器耗尽，或者由于网络而无法达到法定人数）而不得不辞去领导者角色，并说另一个节点 C 成为领导者。

blocks.html_en: • When A steps-down as leader, it aborts all replication threads (including the A—>B catchup) but the leadership transfer goroutine is still blocked waiting for it to complete (an implementation bug).

sentences.en: When A steps-down as leader, it aborts all replication threads (including the A—>B catchup) but the leadership transfer goroutine is still blocked waiting for it to complete (an implementation bug).
sentences.zh: 当 A 不再担任领导者时，它会中止所有复制线程（包括 A—>B 追赶），但领导权转移 goroutine 仍处于阻塞状态，等待其完成（一个实现错误）。

blocks.html_en: There is no problem so far, because C is the new leader and it does its job for a while.

sentences.en: There is no problem so far, because C is the new leader and it does its job for a while.
sentences.zh: 到目前为止还没有问题，因为 C 是新的领导者，它暂时完成了它的工作。

blocks.html_en: • Unfortunately, the leadership transfer goroutine in A has set a global flag “leadership transfer in progress” and this flag cannot be unset until it is unblocked… but it never will be!!!

sentences.en: Unfortunately, the leadership transfer goroutine in A has set a global flag “leadership transfer in progress” and this flag cannot be unset until it is unblocked…
sentences.zh: 不幸的是，A 中的领导权转移 goroutine 设置了一个全局标志“领导权转移正在进行中”，并且该标志在解锁之前无法取消设置......

sentences.en: but it never will be!!!
sentences.zh: 但它永远不会！

blocks.html_en: • Crucially, this flag does not prevent it from participating in elections and the flag does not get reset if it wins a future election.

sentences.en: Crucially, this flag does not prevent it from participating in elections and the flag does not get reset if it wins a future election.
sentences.zh: 至关重要的是，该标志不会阻止其参与选举，并且如果它赢得未来的选举，该标志也不会被重置。

blocks.html_en: • So in the future, A can legitimately get re-elected as leader but it will refuse to accept any client requests and stall on future commits with the reason “leadership transfer in progress”.

sentences.en: So in the future, A can legitimately get re-elected as leader but it will refuse to accept any client requests and stall on future commits with the reason “leadership transfer in progress”.
sentences.zh: 因此，将来，A 可以合法地重新当选为领导者，但它会拒绝接受任何客户端请求，并以“领导权转移正在进行中”为由拖延未来的提交。

blocks.html_en: • When the network is healthy and A is a leader, there is no way to get out of this other than rebooting the node A to clear the flag.

sentences.en: When the network is healthy and A is a leader, there is no way to get out of this other than rebooting the node A to clear the flag.
sentences.zh: 当网络健康并且 A 是领导者时，除了重新启动节点 A 以清除标志之外，没有其他方法可以摆脱这种情况。

blocks.html_en: We caught this using an Antithesis eventually test command that checks for commit progress after fault injection is turned off.

sentences.en: We caught this using an Antithesis eventually test command that checks for commit progress after fault injection is turned off.
sentences.zh: 我们使用 Antithesis 最终测试命令捕获了此问题，该命令在关闭故障注入后检查提交进度。

blocks.html_en: This bug causes a liveness issue: a follower node becomes unable to replicate log entries and is effectively not able to participate in the consensus protocol. The bug can also cause resource exhaustion, where the node starts creating a potentially unbounded number of temporary snapshot files on disk.

blocks.html_en: HashiCorp Raft does not discard the existing log, and so after installing the snapshot its state machine can, in some cases, disagree with the data in its own (stale) log entries.

sentences.en: HashiCorp Raft does not discard the existing log, and so after installing the snapshot its state machine can, in some cases, disagree with the data in its own (stale) log entries.

blocks.html_en: TW Lim Technical Writer

sentences.en: TW Lim Technical Writer
sentences.zh: TW Lim 技术撰稿人

blocks.html_en: If there is a single lesson to be learned here, it’s that formal methods alone cannot ensure that software works, because the formal specification still needs to be implemented, and even if you have mechanized verification, you’re verifying the model and not the implementation itself.

sentences.en: If there is a single lesson to be learned here, it’s that formal methods alone cannot ensure that software works, because the formal specification still needs to be implemented, and even if you have mechanized verification, you’re verifying the model and not the implementation itself.

blocks.html_en: We believe formal methods are useful and necessary — they can confirm the basic soundness of a design, and provide a map that saves engineers from many of the errors that can arise in the implementation of a complex system.

sentences.en: We believe formal methods are useful and necessary — they can confirm the basic soundness of a design, and provide a map that saves engineers from many of the errors that can arise in the implementation of a complex system.

An implementer who misses any of these details is likely to run into trouble.

blocks.html_en: The paper implicitly assumes that each node is a synchronous process, performing atomic state transitions when handling RPCs and updating its own internal state. The TLA+ spec is designed as such.

sentences.en: The paper implicitly assumes that each node is a synchronous process, performing atomic state transitions when handling RPCs and updating its own internal state.
sentences.zh: 该论文隐含地假设每个节点都是一个同步进程，在处理 RPC 时执行原子状态转换并更新其自身的内部状态。

sentences.en: The TLA+ spec is designed as such.
sentences.zh: TLA+ 规范就是这样设计的。

blocks.html_en: At the same time, none of the implementations we’ve looked at have actually been a synchronous process, and there’s no explicit guidance in the implementation guide as to whether and how one can deviate from the synchronous design.

sentences.en: At the same time, none of the implementations we’ve looked at have actually been a synchronous process, and there’s no explicit guidance in the implementation guide as to whether and how one can deviate from the synchronous design.

blocks.html_en: Consider the following situation: Can a leader with an outstanding RPC request respond to a vote, or does it need to wait for a response||timeout? Or should it respond, shut down the request and disregard a future response in order to stay correct?

sentences.en: Or should it respond, shut down the request and disregard a future response in order to stay correct?
sentences.zh: 或者它应该响应、关闭请求并忽略未来的响应以保持正确？

blocks.html_en: HashiCorp Raft is mostly synchronous in handling RPCs, with a single thread in a select loop, except when it isn’t — it does asynchronous heartbeat handling, bypassing its main loop, and this is what allows Bug #1 to creep in.

sentences.en: HashiCorp Raft is mostly synchronous in handling RPCs, with a single thread in a select loop, except when it isn’t — it does asynchronous heartbeat handling, bypassing its main loop, and this is what allows Bug #1 to creep in.
sentences.zh: HashiCorp Raft 在处理 RPC 时大多是同步的，在选择循环中只有一个线程，除非它不是——它进行异步心跳处理，绕过其主循环，这就是允许 Bug #1 潜入的原因。

blocks.html_en: Assumption 2: Each response can be mapped to a request

blocks.html_en: In the Raft paper, every call is made using RPC, which means that every response can be mapped to a request.

blocks.html_en: If one implements Raft on top of simple TCP or UDP, and doesn’t realize that request/response correlation is a crucial part of correctness, bad stuff can easily happen.

sentences.en: If one implements Raft on top of simple TCP or UDP, and doesn’t realize that request/response correlation is a crucial part of correctness, bad stuff can easily happen.

blocks.html_en: If you’re not working in a language with a nice RPC library, it’s not obvious how to establish this correspondence. For example, the Raft authors have a simulation on their website, which for obvious reasons is often considered a demo/canonical implementation even though they’ve never described it as such. But even their own implementation deviates from the protocol and includes an extra matchIndex field in the AppendEntries response in order to avoid matching requests to responses.

content_html_zh:
介绍

TW Lim 技术撰稿人

Raft 共识协议是互联网的基础之一。 Raft 提供了 TLA+ 的正式规范和具体、详细的实现指南，数百个团体已经按照指南中的说明创建了该算法的开源实现。 迄今为止，它是生产系统中使用最广泛的共识算法。

尽管该论文以易于理解的风格着称，但我们在测试过的每个 Raft 实现中都发现了错误，包括 HashiCorp Raft、Aeron Cluster、OpenRaft 和 MicroRaft——尽管我们在正式方法、仔细的代码审查、单元测试和多年的生产测试方面进行了投资。 我们发现的错误表现为违反 Raft 主要不变量（论文中称为状态机安全性，通常在其他地方称为全订单交付）。 如果您使用 Raft 实现，您可能需要检查它是否有错误。

我们已向上游发送错误报告。 这并不是对 Raft、其作者、其实现者或任何特定实现的批评。 Raft 的实现，即使有正式的规范和详细的实现指南，也不容易编写。

相反，这是一个关于分布式系统正确性的故事——错误的不可避免性、任何单一方法的不足以及习得性无助的高昂成本。

这是一篇很长的文章。 第一部分是立场文件，但其余部分是对我们发现的问题的详细分析，以一个实现为例，讨论我们如何发现它们以及为什么我们认为它们存在。

为什么这很重要

如果您曾经在分布式系统上工作过，那么您在某个时候就曾是作战室的一员（如果您没有，别担心，您将会成为），处理像这样的中断，或者这一次的中断 - 两者都是由共识失败引起的。 当共识问题导致事件发生时，找出根本原因、复制和修复不可避免地会影响深远且极其痛苦。 许多共识问题仍然“未解决”，因为它们无法复制。

很难确切地知道这些问题在现实世界中的后果是什么，因为共识协议在堆栈中的位置非常低。 他们是否会破坏某人个人 D&D 游戏的存档？ 核电站存在安全风险？ 德国火车晚点？ 这一切都取决于协议的部署位置。

可以肯定的是，这些错误极大地浪费了开发人员的时间，并影响了数百万甚至数亿用户。

然而，我们接受共识问题和其他深层分布式系统错误作为生活的事实 - 但曾经有一段时间，我们也接受霍乱和等待大型机的出现，作为生活的事实。 开发人员应该得到更好的东西。 每个依赖我们编写的软件的人都应该得到更好的东西。

错误并不是生活中的事实

我们长期以来一直认为共识错误是不可避免的，因为共识协议真的很难正确测试。 要真正彻底地测试 Raft 实现（或任何分布式系统），您实际上需要想象整个堆栈中可能出现问题的每一种可能的情况，并编写一个测试来查看它是否会破坏您的共识协议。 实际上不可能编写足够的测试来在关键系统中提供这种保证。

我们通过两种方式解决这个问题。 首先，我们以中断、下游错误、作战室等形式对用户进行测试。 开发团队不可能编写足够的测试，但是通过足够的部署和足够的用户以及足够的系统配置，您最终会发现所有问题。

其次，我们依赖形式验证，这就是当今共识算法的构建方式。 我们定义一个模型，我们可以在数学上证明它是正确的，然后我们...... 将这个完美的、柏拉图式的东西翻译成代码。 大多数 Raft 实现都是以这种方式构建的。

这里有学位。 Raft 协议是极少数符合最严格的“形式验证”标准的共识协议之一，具有手动证明、模型检查和机械化的正确性证明。 我们知道的每个公共共识协议都有手动证明/书面正确性论证，但只有 Raft、Paxos 和 MultiPaxos 具有机械化证明。

规格不是代码

形式验证是一个很好的起点，因为它有助于确认核心设计是否合理。 在没有从正式规范开始的情况下实现分布式共识协议会导致比任何 Raft 实现更多数量级的错误。

相反，人们可能想知道如果 FoundationDB 团队从正式的规范开始，他们可能会做什么。

但这里的问题表明了从正式规范到实际生产代码所固有的困难。 只要实现是由不可靠、不完美的程序员（无论是人类还是法学硕士）完成的，实际的代码和使用它的系统就只能像实现者的假设一样可靠——而不是正式验证的模型。

此外，正式规范很少是真正完整的——就 Raft 而言，TLA 规范涵盖了核心协议，但没有涉及 installSnapshot、副本替换或处理网络数据包损坏等细节。

测试其实可以很简单

解决这些错误并不需要对共识或分布式系统有特别深入的了解。 我们发现这些使用了一种简单的方法，初级工程师可以在不到一天的时间内实现，这实际上是我们能想到的最简单的状态机复制工作负载。 关键是，这种情况是在系统运行于对立状态时发生的，受到现实环境中发生的故障的影响。

我们想强调这一点，因为我们经常在测试复杂系统时遇到习得性无助。 我们的专业人士认为（有一定道理）为分布式系统编写测试需要比我们更多的专业知识、时间或代币。 这会导致永久的测试不足状态，进而导致开发人员将大量时间浪费在救火上（更不用说精神和情感上的疲惫了）。

开发人员应该得到更好的东西。 每个依赖我们编写的软件的人都应该得到更好的东西。

测试筏

Marco Primi 分布式系统工程师

关于对立

Antithesis 是一个自主测试平台，可在确定性模拟环境中运行分布式系统，并在积极的故障注入下使用随机生成的输入。 要使用 Antithesis，您需要将完整的分布式系统以及工作负载（驱动被测系统的客户端）部署到模拟环境中。

对比将被测系统暴露在模拟环境的安全性生产中将经历的那种不可预测的湍流中。 通过随机化输入和故障，并智能地搜索系统的状态空间，以查看系统不变量是否被违反。

我们维护一个系统和错误的内部课程，用于对 Antithesis 的错误查找性能进行基准测试。 我们一直在课程中添加共识基准，因此我们一直在测试大量 Raft 实现。

构建独特的东西的部分困难在于您还需要构建一种方法来衡量其性能。

关于筏

分布式系统中的常见架构模式是状态机复制（SMR）：系统中的所有副本都运行同一确定性状态机的副本，并且将相同的命令序列传递给所有副本以转换数据/状态。 这会导致副本以软锁步方式进行 - 应用 N 个命令后的状态在所有副本中保持一致，并且所有副本最终应用所有命令。

分布式数据库（FoundationDB、Aerospike等）、消息队列（Kafka、NATS等）、键值存储（etcd、Zookeeper）、区块链（比特币、以太坊）和许多其他系统都是基于SMR的。

实现 SMR 的一个基本要求是所有副本必须以相同的顺序接收相同的命令集——全序交付。 全订单交付很容易描述，但在面对网络动荡、进程崩溃和磁盘故障时很难构建。

由于 SMR 的工作需要保证全订单交付，因此大多数系统都依赖于少数消息传递抽象之一，其中原子广播（也称为全订单广播）是最常见的。 Raft 被视为最友好的原子广播协议，Paxos 和视图标记复制也被广泛使用。

我们的测试方法

为了测试 Raft 实现，我们在 Antithesis 中运行一个 3 节点 Raft 集群，并使用我们称为“区块链”的简单工作负载。

Chain of Blocks 测试了 Raft 最重要的不变量：应用 N 个命令后，所有副本的状态都匹配。 它由两个非常简单的组件组成：

  • 仅对传入命令的字节进行哈希处理的单状态状态机。 在每个应用的命令之后，状态由<应用的命令数，当前散列>组成。 这足以让我们观察副本之间的状态差异。
  • 无状态客户端，其唯一职责是提交由随机字节数组组成的新命令。

您可以在此处阅读有关此工作负载的更多信息，并查看示例实现。

Raft 等组件由专家开发和审查，并经过多年的实践考验。 因此，令我们惊讶的是，这个单一、简单的测试策略——初级工程师可以在一个下午编写（或者克劳德可以为少量代币编写）——在 Antithesis 中运行时仍然会发现错误。

作为一个例子，这里详细介绍了我们在此过程中在一个著名的开源 Raft 实现中发现的错误。 我们强调，我们在其他实现中也发现了类似的错误，但这里要深入而不是广泛，并且仅呈现一组错误以使这篇文章的长度在某种程度上易于管理。

我们计划用我们使用过的其他 Raft 实现中的错误详细信息来更新这篇文章。

HashiCorp 筏

罗汉·帕迪研究员

HashiCorp Raft 是一种成熟、流行的开源 Raft 实现，也是支撑 Consul、Nomad 和 Vault 等广泛使用的生产基础设施工具的基础共识引擎。

我们并不认为 HashiCorp Raft 的可靠性比我们测试的其他实现低，也不认为 HashiCorp Raft 中的错误比其他实现中的错误更严重——它们都违反了状态机安全的相同核心属性。

我们总共发现了三个不同的错误：一个导致大量安全违规（即如上所述的数据分歧），两个导致活动违规（除非操作员干预，否则某些节点或整个集群无法取得进展）。 我们使用的区块链实现在这里。

Raft 技术入门

为了更好地理解这些 bug 的本质，我们应该定义一些在 Raft 论文中经常使用的术语：

  • “Term”、“Leader”、“Follower”、“Election”+“RequestVote”RPC：Raft 通过将协议划分为从 term=1 开始的严格递增的项，确保分布式节点集群之间的共识。 在每个任期中，节点都会尝试通过多数票选出一个节点作为领导者；所有其他节点称为追随者。 领导者选举是使用称为 RequestVote 的远程过程调用 (RPC) 进行的。
  • “Log”、“Commit”、“Replication” + “AppendEntries” RPC：每个节点维护一个数据条目的复制日志（例如客户端发出的命令），其中一些前缀被称为已提交；也就是说，当条目提交时，节点的状态机就会更新。 当客户端向集群发送某些命令时，只有当前领导者可以服务该请求，并且领导者通过称为 AppendEntries 的 RPC 将关联的数据条目复制到其所有追随者。 当集群中的大多数节点在其日志中复制相同的数据条目时，领导者会将其提交到自己的状态机并将此事实广播给其追随者。 如果一些追随者节点由于网络故障而落后，或者如果他们的条目日志中有之前任期未提交的数据，那么当前领导者总是可以通过更多的 AppendEntries RPC 赶上他们。 AppendEntries RPC 还用作常规心跳机制来广播领导者处于活动状态。
  • “Compaction”、“Snapshot”+“InstallSnapshot”RPC：当条目日志变得太大时，Raft 节点可以选择压缩日志中所有已提交的条目，并仅在磁盘上存储该点之前状态机的快照。 如果领导节点需要通过 AppendEntries 将数据条目复制到追随者，但其日志已被压缩，则可以发出 InstallSnapshot RPC 将整个状态机传输到追随者。

Bug 1 - 由于异步心跳导致共识被打破

这是我们发现的最严重的错误。 它会影响 Raft 纸的五种安全特性中的四种（图 3）：

  • 日志匹配（通过机制 A 违反 - 在上面的报告中看到）
  • 领导者完整性（通过机制 A 违反 - 如上面的报告所示）

  • 选举安全（通过机制 B 违反 - 不在上面显示的报告中）

根本原因和触发因素
  • Raft 论文假设所有操作（处理 RPC、客户端请求、选举等）都是原子的，并且不会相互交错。 本质上，协议中的每个节点都是一个有限状态机。
  • 在 HashiCorp raft 中，大多数状态更改操作都是由主线程中的大型 switch-loop 处理的，其他几个浮动 goroutine 执行不影响协议状态的异步工作（例如，用于分派追加条目的点对点“复制”例程，以及监听传入 RPC 并将其交给主线程进行处理的每个连接“传输”goroutine）。
  • 除了有一个与协议不同的优化：传入的心跳消息（即没有条目的 AppendEntries）在 I/O“传输”线程本身上处理，而不是像其他 RPC 那样将其排队等待主线程循环。 据推测，这是为了快速重置保活定时器并减少虚假重选。
  • 需要注意的是，传入的心跳消息（像任何其他 AppendEntries RPC 一样）如果在其他人当选为领导者时携带新术语，则可以更改状态，这会提高主线程中其他所有内容所依赖的全局 currentTerm，并将当前状态设置为 FOLLOWER。 与主线程同时执行这些状态更改绝对是不合理的，并且可能会导致不同类型的竞争条件错误。
机制 A - 主线程上使用dispatchLogs() 进行传入心跳竞赛

以下是该错误如何导致 3 节点设置 A/B/C 中出现分歧的原因：

  • 假设节点 A 和节点 B 之间的网络链路已关闭。
  • 节点 A 成为任期 T 的候选人，请求投票（最终从节点 C 获得投票）
  • 节点 B 也竞选 T 任期，但没有投票
  • 节点 B 成为 T+1 任期的候选人，请求投票（从节点 C 获取）
  • 节点 B 赢得 T+1 任期选举
  • 节点 A 赢得任期 T 的选举（刚刚收到节点 C 的旧投票）
  • 节点 B 发出 term=T+1 的心跳 AppendEntries，节点 A 没有立即收到
  • 节点 A 收到客户端申请新数据条目 X 的​​请求，并且它仍然认为自己是 term T 的领导者，因此在主线程上它准备创建一个日志条目（data=X，term=T）并向对等节点发送 AppendEntries。 然而：就在它可以创建日志条目之前，节点 B 在上述步骤 7 中发送的心跳到达，设置 currentTerm=T+1。 因为这是在网络传输线程的快速路径上完成的，所以它与主线程竞争。 主线程最终准备一个日志条目（data=X，term=T+1），并在下一个主循环迭代之前用这些值调度 AppendEntries，它意识到它现在实际上是 term T+1 的追随者。
  • 从这里开始事情变得非常糟糕。 一些节点将这个伪造的 data=X, term=T+1 应用于其日志，而其他节点则遵循节点 B（term T+1 的真正领导者）所说的任何内容，例如，它们可能在与 term=T+1 相同的索引处应用 data=Y。 日志在数据上有所不同，但会被提交，因为所有日志都表示同一索引的术语 T+1。 状态机存在分歧。
机制 B - 主线程上使用 requestVote() 进行传入心跳竞赛

当异步心跳处理程序与主线程上的 RequestVote RPC 的并发处理程序竞争时，相同的错误可能会导致另一种安全违规。 如果传入的心跳和 RequestVote 分别携带编号较大但不同的术语 T1 和 T2（当接收方刚刚从故障中恢复并正在追赶来自对等方的排队消息时，这是可能的）并且如果 T1 小于 T2，则接收方可能 (i) 意识到心跳的术语 T1 高于其当前术语，然后 (2) 在处理 RequestVote 的主线程上意识到 T2 高于其当前术语，因此将其当前术语设置为T2然后授予投票权；然后 (3) 返回心跳处理程序的线程，将其当前项设置为较低的值 T1。 不用说，对术语 T2 进行投票的节点永远不可能将其当前术语回归到较低的值 T1！ 当该节点在稍后某个时刻再次将其任期增加到 T2 时，它不记得自己已经在该任期中投票了。

综上所述，竞争最终会导致一个节点在同一任期内授予两票（上面的 T2），这在最坏的情况下可能会导致两个不同的节点在同一任期内被选为领导者！ 以下是当我们观察到这种竞争条件及其违反选举安全时来自 HashiCorp Raft 的一些示例日志消息：

Bug 2 - 领导权转移后陷入僵局

此错误会导致活性问题——在集群正常运行时，领导节点无法服务客户端请求或提交新条目。 根本原因是领导权转移操作（Consul 使用的 Raft 协议扩展，您可以要求当前领导者将领导权转移给其他人，例如升级）期间的死锁，它不会立即发出任何警告信号，而是让整个集群陷入困境，从而让您陷入未来。

  • 当您启动从 A 到 B 的领导权转移时，当前领导者 A 首先尝试通过异步复制线程使 B 的日志保持最新。
  • 领导权转移逻辑是一个单独的 goroutine，它在告诉 B 接管之前等待此复制。
  • 当这一切发生时，A 可能不得不因为不相关的原因（例如，租约计时器耗尽，或者由于网络而无法达到法定人数）而不得不辞去领导者角色，并说另一个节点 C 成为领导者。
  • 当 A 不再担任领导者时，它会中止所有复制线程（包括 A—>B 追赶），但领导权转移 goroutine 仍处于阻塞状态，等待其完成（一个实现错误）。

到目前为止还没有问题，因为 C 是新的领导者，它暂时完成了它的工作。

  • 不幸的是，A 中的领导权转移 goroutine 设置了一个全局标志“领导权转移正在进行中”，并且该标志在解锁之前无法取消设置...... 但它永远不会！
  • 至关重要的是，该标志不会阻止其参与选举，并且如果它赢得未来的选举，该标志也不会被重置。
  • 因此，将来，A 可以合法地重新当选为领导者，但它会拒绝接受任何客户端请求，并以“领导权转移正在进行中”为由拖延未来的提交。
  • 当网络健康并且 A 是领导者时，除了重新启动节点 A 以清除标志之外，没有其他方法可以摆脱这种情况。

Bug 3 - 快照安装中的活锁

此错误会导致活性问题：追随者节点无法复制日志条目，并且实际上无法参与共识协议。 该错误还可能导致资源耗尽，节点开始在磁盘上创建可能无限数量的临时快照文件。

这个 bug 的根本原因非常简单：在我们测试的 HashiCorp Raft 版本中，InstallSnapshot RPC 的实现根本不遵循 Raft 论文中图 13 中的规则 7，该规则处理传入快照表示与接收者未提交日志条目不同的状态的情况。 在论文中，规则 7 说：

“丢弃整个日志”

HashiCorp Raft 不会丢弃现有日志，因此在安装快照后，在某些情况下，其状态机可能与其自己的（陈旧）日志条目中的数据不一致。

起初，这听起来可能是良性的，因为状态机应该是最终的事实来源。 然而，当节点从领导者接收到后续的 AppendEntries RPC 时，它会忠实地实现协议的一部分（规则 2），即：“如果日志在 prevLogIndex 处不包含其术语与 prevLogTerm 匹配的条目，则[拒绝 AppendEntries]”。 因此，由于日志陈旧，追随者会拒绝后续的 AppendEntries，导致领导者以新的 InstallSnapshot 进行响应，并且此循环将永远持续下去。

反思

TW Lim 技术撰稿人

如果说这里有一个教训值得吸取的话，那就是仅靠形式化方法并不能确保软件能够正常工作，因为形式化规范仍然需要实现，即使你有机械化验证，你也是在验证模型而不是实现本身。

我们相信形式化方法是有用且必要的——它们可以确认设计的基本合理性，并提供一个地图，使工程师避免在复杂系统的实现中可能出现的许多错误。

但正如这些错误所表明的那样，在将正式规范转换为生产代码时，错误不断出现。 在我们使用各种 Raft 实现的过程中，我们发现了 Raft 论文中仍然隐含的许多假设。 错过任何这些细节的实施者都可能会遇到麻烦。

假设1：每个节点都是一个同步进程

Marco Primi 分布式系统工程师

该论文隐含地假设每个节点都是一个同步进程，在处理 RPC 时执行原子状态转换并更新其自身的内部状态。 TLA+ 规范就是这样设计的。

与此同时，我们所研究的实现实际上都不是同步过程，并且实现指南中没有关于是否以及如何偏离同步设计的明确指导。

考虑以下情况：具有未完成的 RPC 请求的领导者是否可以响应投票，或者是否需要等待响应||超时？ 或者它应该响应、关闭请求并忽略未来的响应以保持正确？

HashiCorp Raft 在处理 RPC 时大多是同步的，在选择循环中只有一个线程，除非它不是——它进行异步心跳处理，绕过其主循环，这就是允许 Bug #1 潜入的原因。

假设 2：每个响应都可以映射到一个请求

在Raft论文中，每个调用都是使用RPC进行的，这意味着每个响应都可以映射到一个请求。

如果一个人在简单的 TCP 或 UDP 之上实现 Raft，并且没有意识到请求/响应相关性是正确性的关键部分，那么很容易发生不好的事情。

如果您使用的语言没有很好的 RPC 库，那么如何建立这种对应关系并不明显。 例如，Raft 作者在他们的网站上有一个模拟，由于显而易见的原因，该模拟通常被认为是演示/规范实现，尽管他们从未这样描述过。 但即使他们自己的实现也偏离了协议，并在 AppendEntries 响应中包含了一个额外的 matchIndex 字段，以避免将请求与响应匹配。

假设3：currentTerm和votedFor一致

罗汉·帕迪研究员

Raft 论文的图 2 指出：

一个关键假设是 currentTerm 和 votedFor 是一致的，因为后者记录了当前任期的投票。 如果这些不同步，就会发生不好的事情，特别是如果 votedFor 为空。

为了安全起见，应以原子方式将这些值写入持久存储。 但在协议中，这些值实际上在不同的地方发生变化，因此确保两个值一起更新是很微妙的。

JavaScript 中的在线模拟器实际上并不区分持久状态和内存中状态，因此没有如何执行此操作的“参考实现”。

例如，HashiCorp Raft 偏离了协议，以非原子方式存储了 currentTerm、lastVoteTerm 和 lastVoteCand 的三个独立值，最坏情况下会对性能造成风险，但不会带来安全风险（即，它可能会保留更新的 lastVoteTerm，然后在更新 lastVoteCand 之前崩溃，但当它重新启动时，它只会对该术语进行预先确定的投票，而不是像平常一样选择候选人）。

结论

TW Lim 技术撰稿人

我们长期以来一直认为错误是不可避免的。 分布式系统几乎不可能进行彻底的测试，因为它们的状态空间非常大，并且随着我们的堆栈变得越来越复杂，问题只会变得更糟。

但技术进步也推动了可能性的前沿。 我们通过建设水处理厂和污水处理系统消灭了发达国家的霍乱。 我们不再等待大型机，因为我们已经使计算能力变得廉价且丰富。

计算的丰富性是最近才出现的现象。 这句话可能在过去 15 年里一直成立，还不到计算历史的十分之一。 除其他外，最近人们对形式验证的兴趣激增——希望机械化证明和模型检查最终能够变得足够简单、足够便宜，以便我们能够在任何需要的地方应用这些方法。 但我们在 Raft 方面的经验表明，即使经过机械验证的模型的实现也可能存在缺陷，因为没有机械方法来检查实现者的假设。

幸运的是，廉价且丰富的计算也使得以我们以前无法做到的方式测试软件成为可能。 我们对 Raft 的测试表明的另一件事是，当您在故障下运行系统时，即使是基本的测试方法也会揭示出以前需要数月的手动测试才能发现的问题。

开发人员应该得到更好的东西，每个依赖我们软件的人也应该得到更好的东西。
